title: Transmission pathways in residential aged care
audience: Cleaners and cleaning supervisors working in residential aged care in any Australian state or territory. This lesson builds awareness of how infection moves in a care home. It does not teach diagnosis or clinical precautions.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: NHMRC, Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019) (no page date shown; document dated 2019); Aged Care Act 2024: news and commencement (no date shown).
learningOutcomes: Describe contact, droplet and airborne transmission in plain terms, and state how they affect environmental cleaning.
Explain why the cleaner does not diagnose infection, identify a transmission route, or select a precaution.
Identify high-risk features of a residential aged care setting, such as shared spaces, high-touch surfaces and frail residents, that increase the importance of cleaning.
State the referral route when staff report new symptoms in a resident or a colleague.

instruction.heading: Why cleaners need to understand transmission
instruction.body: Infections move from person to person and from surfaces to people by a few main routes. A cleaner who understands these routes can do the environmental part of their job well: clean the places where contamination collects, avoid carrying it from one room to another, and stop when a risk is not in the plan. Understanding transmission does not mean diagnosing anyone, deciding which precautions a resident needs, or telling staff or families what a symptom means. Those decisions belong to the clinical team and the infection prevention and control team, and the facility's current instructions set what applies.

instruction.heading: Contact, droplet and airborne routes in plain terms
instruction.body: Contact transmission happens when an organism passes from a person or a surface to another person's hands or body, often through touch. Droplet transmission happens when larger droplets from a cough, sneeze or close conversation reach another person's eyes, nose or mouth, usually over a short distance. Airborne transmission happens when smaller particles stay suspended in the air and can be carried further in a room or through ventilation. In residential aged care the first route is the most common concern for cleaners, because touched surfaces, shared equipment and hand contact carry the organism between people. Which precautions apply for each route in a given case is decided by clinical staff, not by the cleaner.

instruction.heading: Why a care home is a higher-risk setting
instruction.body: Residents in residential aged care are often older and frail, may have reduced immunity or existing health conditions, and share bathrooms, dining rooms, lounges and corridors. Staff move between rooms many times a shift, and handrails, door handles, call bells and shared equipment are touched by many people. These features make environmental cleaning more important, and they also make it important that a cleaner does not carry a contamination from one resident's room into another. Plan the work from the most protected area to the most exposed, and never move from a room with a known risk to a clean room without the procedure for that situation.

instruction.heading: What to do when symptoms are reported
instruction.body: A resident or colleague may report new symptoms, or a carer may tell you that someone is unwell. Do not diagnose, do not name an infection, and do not tell anyone whether the symptoms are serious. Protect residents by following the current instructions, stop any task that would bring you into a risk you have not been trained for, and tell the nurse or the infection prevention contact immediately. If a notice is posted on the room, read it, follow it, and do not remove it. Record the report you made, the time and the person you told. The clinical team decides what happens next.

instruction.heading: Worked scenario: symptoms after the schedule was printed
instruction.body: A care unit reports new respiratory symptoms in several residents after the room cleaning schedule was printed. You are booked to clean three rooms on the unit. The first step is not to start work from the printed schedule as if nothing has changed. Ask the nurse in charge for the current instruction for the unit, and do not infer a cause from the symptoms. Follow the instruction you are given, and if the instruction changes the rooms, the sequence or the products, confirm it in writing before you start. Record the instruction you followed, who gave it, and the time.

procedure: Read the current facility notice for the unit before starting, and check it against the printed schedule.
Plan the route from less exposed areas to more exposed areas, as the facility procedure directs.
Identify the touch points in the area and keep clean supplies away from used items.
If any resident or colleague reports symptoms, do not diagnose or classify them. Stop the affected task and tell the nurse or IPC contact.
Follow the current instruction for the unit, and confirm any change in writing before acting on it.
Record any report, instruction and change, with the time and the person you told.

workedExamples.situation: You are cleaning a resident room. The resident's carer says the resident has a cough and asks whether they should be worried and whether you can go into the next room now.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you say and do?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not diagnose or reassure. Say that you will pass the concern to the nurse, and stop the room work at a safe point. Tell the nurse the same moment and ask for the current instruction before entering the next room. Record the report, the nurse you told, and the time. Do not move on to the next room until the instruction is confirmed.

workedExamples.situation: A notice on a resident's door says that additional precautions apply, but the printed schedule has you cleaning the room as usual.
workedExamples.reasoning: Follow the current instruction on the door and the nurse's direction, not the printed schedule. Confirm with the nurse what the precautions require for your task, including entry, equipment and product. Do not remove the notice. Record the instruction and the time.

equipmentAndPpe: Current facility notice or unit instruction for each area
Protective equipment for the task as set by the facility: {{business:safety.required_ppe}}
Facility contact for infection prevention and control: {{business:safety.escalation_contact}}

commonErrors.error: Telling a resident or family member what a symptom means or whether it is an infection.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not diagnose. Pass the concern to the nurse and record it.

commonErrors.error: Following the printed schedule when a current notice or instruction says something different.
commonErrors.prevention: The current instruction governs. Check the notice on the door and with the nurse before starting.

commonErrors.error: Moving straight from a known-risk room into a clean room with the same cloth or equipment.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the facility route and keep used items separate. Stop if the route is unclear.

commonErrors.error: Assuming that a clean room is free of risk, because it looks clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Visible cleanliness does not show whether an organism is present. Follow the plan, not appearance.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Cleaning staff do not diagnose infections and do not select transmission-based precautions for residents. Those decisions are made by clinical staff and the infection prevention and control team under the facility's governance, as set out in the NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019).
The specific precaution categories, their names and the criteria for applying them in Australian residential aged care, were not extracted in this draft.

Residential aged care operates under the Aged Care Act 2024, which commenced on 1 November 2025, together with the strengthened Aged Care Quality Standards. The facility's infection prevention procedures are its own obligation under those standards.

qualityStandard: The learner describes contact, droplet and airborne transmission in their own words without naming a specific infection.
The learner gives the correct response to two supplied symptom reports, without diagnosing or classifying the symptoms.
The learner states which instruction governs when a printed schedule conflicts with a current notice.
The learner records a symptom report with the person told and the time.
documentationEvidence: Record of any symptom report made, the person told, and the time
The current instruction followed for the unit, and who gave it
Any change to the planned route, sequence or product, confirmed in writing
summary: Contact, droplet and airborne routes affect how cleaners plan and protect their work.
Cleaners do not diagnose, do not select precautions, and do not tell residents what a symptom means.
When symptoms are reported, follow the current instruction, stop the affected task, and tell the nurse or IPC contact.
Record every report and instruction followed.

knowledgeChecks.question: A carer says a resident has a cough and asks whether you can go into the next room. What should you do?
options: Do not diagnose. Stop at a safe point, tell the nurse, and wait for the current instruction before entering the next room.
Tell the carer the cough is probably nothing and go on to the next room, since a cough is a common issue here
Clean the next room quickly and leave the first room for the nurse to check when they are free later in the shift

knowledgeChecks.question: The printed schedule and a notice on the door conflict. Which should you follow?
options: The printed schedule, because it was issued first and is the official record
The current notice and the nurse's instruction, which govern the task.
Whichever is easier to carry out in the time available on the shift

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement best describes the cleaner's role in transmission?
options: Cleaners decide which precautions a resident needs based on their own judgement of the room, the risk and the resident's history
Cleaners are responsible for diagnosing residents who report symptoms to them during the clean on the day
Cleaners reduce environmental contamination and carry out the facility's instructions, without diagnosing or selecting precautions.
